tip: Past-tense doers take ने (ne): श्याम ने नई नौकरी शुरू की (Shyam ne naee naukree shuru kee = Shyam started a new job). Ne appears only when the action lands on something.
No ने (ne) on the doer here: विकास (Vikas) just गया (gayaa = went). Going acts on nothing, so the doer stays plain. Ne appears only when the action lands on a thing.
ख़रीदी (khareedee) ends in -ee because मछली (machhlee = fish) is feminine – with ne the verb matches the thing bought, not the buyer. Anil's own gender never touches it.
बेच दीं (bech deen = sold off) ends in a nasal sound because किताबें (kitaaben = books) is feminine plural – the verb tracks the books, and the tiny dot is its only plural clue.
'Reached Shimla' sounds like it acts on Shimla, but पहुँच गए (pahunch gaye) takes no ने (ne) – arriving counts as pure motion in Hindi, like going and coming.
'Told me to rest' = आराम करने को कहा (aaraam karne ko kahaa) – literally 'said for doing rest'. Orders and requests use karne ko, not a plain to-verb.
खा लिया (khaa liyaa) adds लेना (lenaa = take) to eating – it signals the food is finished, gone. Plain खाया (khaayaa) just says eating happened, with no sense of completion.
भेज दिया (bhej diyaa) adds देना (denaa = give) to 'sent' – the give part marks the job fully done, aimed at someone else. A bare भेजा (bhejaa) feels unfinished.
दवाई खिलाई (davaaee khilaaee) is literally 'fed the medicine' – खिलाना (khilaanaa) means making someone eat. In Hindi, patients are fed medicine, not given it.
Hindi has no verb 'drive' – you make the vehicle go: गाड़ी तेज़ चलाई (gaadee tez chalaaee = drove the car fast). चलाना (chalaanaa = make move) also runs shops and machines.
कराया (karaayaa) = got it done by someone else: रिचार्ज कराया (recharge karaayaa) – the shop recharged it, I arranged it. किया (kiyaa) would mean I did it myself.
No 'was inspected' – Hindi says the check happened: जाँच हुई (jaanch huee = inspection happened). When the doer doesn't matter, things simply occur.
Joy happens TO you in Hindi: ख़ुशी हुई (khushee huee = happiness occurred). You aren't glad – gladness arrived. The set phrase for being pleased to meet someone.
'Without' wraps its noun from both sides: बिना किसी मदद के (binaa kisee madad ke) – binaa before, ke after. English says 'without' once; Hindi closes the bracket.
The ending -कर (-kar) means 'having done it': ढोल बजाकर (dhol bajaakar = having beaten the drum). One small ending does the work of English 'by ...ing'.
-ते हुए (-te hue) = 'while doing': नाव खेते हुए (naav khete hue = while rowing the boat). Two actions in one sentence, no word for 'while' needed.
वाला (vaalaa) turns any noun into 'the one with it': ऑटो वाले (auto vaale) = the auto guy. Chai vaalaa, rickshaw vaalaa – it names people by what they run.
Hindi pairs its linking words: जिस किसान ने (jis kisaan ne = the farmer who) opens, उसकी (uskee = that one's) answers. English drops the second half – Hindi says both.
You don't 'like' things in Hindi – they come to your liking: पसंद आया (pasand aayaa = came to liking). The dosa does the arriving; you just receive it.
नाना-नानी (naanaa-naanee) means specifically your mother's parents – your father's are दादा-दादी (daadaa-daadee). Hindi has no plain 'grandparents'; the side always shows.
Doubling intensifies: सुबह-सुबह (subah-subah = morning-morning) means very early, at the crack of dawn. Repeating a word is a normal grammar move in Hindi.
You ask FROM someone: वेटर से बिल माँगा (vetar se bil maangaa = asked the bill from the waiter). माँगना (maangnaa = ask for) always takes se, never ko.
English words become verbs with किया (kiyaa = did): बुक किया (buk kiyaa) = booked. The loanword stays a noun; करना (karnaa = to do) does the verb work – recharge kiyaa, cancel kiyaa.
One respected man, plural verb: वे रिटायर हो गए (ve retire ho gaye = they retired) said of a single person. Respect turns he into they, and the verb agrees.
जी (jee) after a name adds warmth and respect: सुनीता जी (Suneetaa jee). It attaches to any name – and even to yes and no: haan jee, nahin jee.
